front: Why is a chain of thought 'inference compute'?
back: Each generated token costs one forward pass, so writing more reasoning tokens spends more computation on the question.
Extract the final answer, normalise its notation, check equivalence with the reference, then average over the dataset.

front: How to extract `\boxed{...}` with nested braces
back: Find the last `\boxed`, skip spaces, expect `{`, scan forward with a depth counter (+1 on `{`, -1 on `}`) until depth 0; return None if it never balances.

front: Extraction fallbacks and when to use them
back: Last number, whole text, or nothing. Forgiving fallbacks suit measurement; a strict box-only rule suits training rewards because it teaches the format.
A deterministic, automatic reward such as r = 1 if the extracted answer is equivalent to the reference else 0; no learned reward model needed.
Exact rationals compared exactly (0.3333333333 is not 1/3); irrational values (sqrt) compared with a tight relative tolerance. Choose and document the policy.

front: Why compare tuples part by part
back: (2,1) is not (1,2); the order and the number of parts must match, and each pair is checked for equivalence.
The probability that at least one of k sampled answers is correct; with success rate p and independent samples it equals 1-(1-p)^k.
From n samples with c correct: 1 - C(n-c, k) / C(n, k); equals 1 when n-c < k.
1 - prod_{i=n-c+1}^{n} (1 - k/i), algebraically identical to the binomial form but safe for large n.
(1-x)^k is convex, so Jensen gives E[(1-c/n)^k] >= (1-p)^k; the plug-in underestimates pass@k.
sqrt(p(1-p)/N); for 48.2% on 500 problems about 2.2 points, so a 95% interval is about plus or minus 4.4 points.

front: Why Wilson instead of estimate plus/minus 1.96 SE
back: At rates near 0 or 1 or with small N the normal interval can leave [0,1]; Wilson stays inside and has better coverage.
